blocks.robotComment: Readable code that's fast to write — that's Python's whole pitch. Let's see how it pulls that off. 🐍
blocks.body: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. It's built around a simple idea: code should be easy to read and easy to write, so more of your time goes into solving problems instead of fighting the language's syntax.

Python is an interpreted language. Instead of compiling your entire program into a separate file before you can run it — the way Java is compiled into bytecode with a distinct build step — a program called the Python interpreter reads your code and runs it directly, statement by statement. This makes the edit-and-run cycle very fast: you save a file and run it immediately, with no separate compilation step of your own to trigger.

code.code: print("Hello, World!")
code.caption: This single line is a complete, runnable Python program — no class, no method, and nothing to compile before running it.

blocks.robotComment: Get the indentation wrong here and Python won't just judge your style — it'll change what runs. 👀
blocks.body: One of Python's most distinctive features is that it uses whitespace — specifically, indentation — to mark blocks of code, instead of curly braces {} like Java. If you indent a line incorrectly, Python won't just complain about style: it can change what your code actually does, or refuse to run at all. This forces every Python program to be laid out consistently, which makes code easier for you — and everyone else — to read.

blocks.sentence: Instead of curly braces, Python uses ___ to mark blocks of code, such as the body of a loop or function.
blocks.explanation: Python groups code into blocks using consistent indentation (spaces), rather than curly braces or keywords.

blocks.body: Python is also a general-purpose language, meaning it isn't built for just one job. It's one of the most popular languages for web development (with frameworks like Django and Flask), data science and machine learning (with libraries like pandas and NumPy), automating repetitive tasks and writing scripts, and even building simple games and desktop tools.

blocks.explanation: The Python interpreter executes your code directly. This is different from languages like Java, where you compile source code into a separate form before running it.

blocks.robotComment: Every language has an origin story — this one starts with a bored guy on Christmas break. 🎄
blocks.body: Python's story starts around Christmas 1989, when a Dutch programmer named Guido van Rossum began working on a hobby project to keep himself busy over the holidays. He wanted a language that was easier and more enjoyable to write than the tools he used at work — readable, with a gentle learning curve.

blocks.question: Who created Python?
blocks.explanation: Guido van Rossum began working on Python as a personal project around the end of 1989.

blocks.body: The name itself has nothing to do with snakes. Van Rossum was a fan of the British comedy show "Monty Python's Flying Circus," and wanted a name that was short, unique, and a little mysterious — so he picked Python. The logo's two intertwined snakes came later, as a playful nod to the name.

blocks.sentence: Python was named after the comedy group Monty ___.
blocks.explanation: The language is named after Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the animal — Guido van Rossum was simply a fan of the show.

blocks.body: Python 1.0 was released in 1994. Since then, the language has grown steadily: Python 2 arrived in 2000, and Python 3 — a deliberately backwards-incompatible redesign meant to fix long-standing inconsistencies — arrived in 2008. Python 2 support officially ended in 2020, so every Python you write today is Python 3.

Python is developed as an open-source project today, guided by the Python Software Foundation, with contributions from thousands of volunteers around the world — nobody owns it the way a single company owns some other languages.

🔬 Scientific computing: Researchers in physics, biology, and other sciences often use Python to run simulations and analyze experimental results, since it's approachable for people who aren't primarily software engineers.

blocks.robotComment: No setup ceremony here — a Python program can be one line in one file. Let's write it. 🐍
blocks.body: A Python program is simply a plain text file saved with a .py extension, such as hello.py. There is nothing more you need to set up before you can start writing actual, working code inside it.

This is quite different from Java, where every runnable program must live inside a class, with a public static void main(String[] args) method acting as the required entry point — boilerplate you have to write before a single line of your own logic runs. Python has no such requirement: a file can contain just one line, and that line is the entire program.

code.code: print("Hello, World!")
code.caption: Save this single line in a file named hello.py — that is the entire program. No class, no main method, nothing else needed.

blocks.robotComment: No main() to hunt for — Python just starts at line one and goes. 🐍
blocks.body: When you run a Python file, the interpreter reads it from top to bottom and executes each statement in the order it appears. There is no special starting point you need to declare, like main() in Java — the first line of the file is simply the first thing that runs.

blocks.sentence: Unlike Java, a runnable Python program does not need to be wrapped in a ___ or a main method.
blocks.explanation: Python files run top to bottom as-is — there is no requirement to define a class or a main method before your code can execute.

blocks.body: By convention, Python files use lowercase names, with underscores separating words if needed — for example hello_world.py rather than HelloWorld.py. This lowercase, underscore-separated style (called snake_case) shows up throughout Python, not just in file names.

blocks.question: What must every Java program have that a Python program does not?

blocks.explanation: Java requires a class with a main() method as the fixed entry point. Python has no such requirement — a file just runs from top to bottom.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Trust the top-to-bottom rule here.

blocks.robotComment: print() is the very first tool you'll reach for, over and over. 🐍
blocks.body: The print() function displays output in the terminal — it is how a Python program communicates with whoever is running it. You give print() the value you want to show by placing it inside the parentheses, and it can display text, whole numbers, decimals, and more.

code.code:
print("Hello!")
print(42)
print(3.14)
code.caption: print() can display a piece of text in quotes, a whole number, or a decimal number, each on its own line.

blocks.body: print() can also accept several values at once, separated by commas. When you do this, print() automatically places a single space between each value and joins everything into one line of output.

code.code:
name = "Ada"
age = 36
print("Name:", name, "Age:", age)
code.caption: Passing several values separated by commas. This prints: Name: Ada Age: 36

blocks.robotComment: These two keyword arguments quietly control more of your output formatting than you might expect. 🖨️
blocks.body: You can customize how print() joins multiple values using its sep keyword argument, which stands for "separator" — by default it is a single space (" "). You can also control what print() adds after everything is printed using its end keyword argument, which defaults to a newline character ("\n"), moving the cursor down to the next line for whatever gets printed next.

code.code:
print("a", "b", "c", sep="-")
print("Hi", end="")
print(" there!")
code.caption: sep="-" joins the values with dashes instead of spaces, printing "a-b-c". end="" removes the usual newline, so "Hi" and " there!" end up on the same line: "Hi there!"

blocks.sentence: By default, the sep keyword argument of print() places a single ___ between each value you pass to it.
blocks.explanation: Unless you override it, print() automatically joins multiple values with a single space.

options: What gets printed after the values, instead of the default newline
What gets printed before the values

blocks.explanation: end controls what print() outputs after its values. By default this is a newline character, which is why each call to print() normally starts on a fresh line.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Check what happens without any override here.
blocks.statement: By default, print() automatically starts a new line after printing its output.
blocks.explanation: The end argument defaults to "\n" (a newline character), so each print() call moves to a new line by default unless you override it.

blocks.robotComment: Comments are the one part of your code Python never even looks at. 🐍
blocks.body: A comment is a note in your code that Python completely ignores when it runs. Comments exist purely for humans — to explain why a piece of code exists, or what a tricky line is actually doing — not for the interpreter.

code.code:
# This calculates the discounted price
price = 100
discounted = price * 0.8  # apply a 20% discount
code.caption: A # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. Everything after it is ignored when the program runs.

blocks.robotComment: One symbol, every time — refreshingly simple compared to some languages. 💬
blocks.body: Unlike Java's // and /* */, Python only has this one comment style. To comment out several lines in a row, you simply start each one with its own #.

code.code:

# Step 2: validate it
# Step 3: process it
value = input()
code.caption: Stacking # on consecutive lines is Python's way of writing a multi-line comment — there's no separate block-comment syntax.

blocks.sentence: In Python, a comment starts with the ___ symbol and runs to the end of the line.
blocks.explanation: Python uses # for comments — there is no separate multi-line comment syntax like /* */.

blocks.body: Good comments explain the why, not the what. print("Hi")  # prints Hi is a useless comment — the code already says that clearly. A comment earns its place when it explains a reason that isn't obvious from the code itself, like why a particular number or approach was chosen.

blocks.robotComment: Variables here skip the type keyword entirely — Python just watches what you hand it. 🐍
blocks.body: A variable is a named container that stores a piece of data your program can work with and change while it runs. In Python, you never declare a type for a variable — the general pattern is simply name = value, and Python figures out what kind of data it is automatically. This is called dynamic typing: a variable's type is determined by whatever value it currently holds, and that can even change later if you assign it something new.

code.code:
age = 25
print(age)
code.caption: Creating a variable named age, giving it the value 25, and then printing it. No type keyword needed.

blocks.robotComment: score and Score are two totally different variables here — case really does matter. 🐍
blocks.body: Variable names in Python must start with a letter or an underscore (_) — never a digit — and can't be one of Python's reserved keywords (like if or class). Names are case-sensitive, so score and Score are two different variables. By convention, Python developers write variable names in snake_case: all lowercase, with underscores separating words, e.g. total_score or first_name.

blocks.sentence: Python's naming convention for variables is ___, where words are lowercase and separated by underscores, such as total_score.
blocks.explanation: Python's style guide (PEP 8) recommends snake_case for variable names — all lowercase, words joined with underscores.

blocks.body: A variable can also be reassigned: given a new value after it already has one. The new value simply replaces the old one, and unlike statically typed languages, the new value does not even need to be the same type as before — a variable that held a number can later hold text.

code.code:
lives = 3
lives = lives - 1
print(lives)  # 2

lives = "game over"
print(lives)  # now a string, and that's fine
code.caption: Reassigning a variable using its own current value, then reassigning it again to a completely different type.

blocks.body: Python also lets you assign several variables at once on a single line by separating both the names and the values with commas. This is called multiple assignment, and it is a common, tidy way to set up related variables together.

code.code:
a, b = 1, 2
print(a)  # 1
print(b)  # 2

name, age, is_student = "Maya", 21, True
code.caption: Multiple assignment creates several variables in one line, matching each name to the value in the same position.

blocks.question: What happens when you reassign a Python variable to a value of a different type than it held before?
options: It works fine — the variable now holds the new value and its new type
The old value and type are kept alongside the new one
The program crashes when it runs
blocks.explanation: Python variables aren't locked to a type — reassigning simply makes the variable point to whatever new value you give it.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Think about what a Python variable declaration actually looks like.
blocks.statement: In Python, you must write a type keyword before a variable name when creating it, similar to int in other languages.
blocks.explanation: Python has no type keyword for variables — you simply write name = value, and Python infers the type from the value.

blocks.robotComment: Two number types, zero type keywords to write — Python figures it out from the value itself. 🐍
blocks.body: Python has two main number types you'll use constantly: int for whole numbers (no decimal point) and float for numbers with a decimal point. You never declare which one a variable is — Python decides based on how you write the value.

code.code:
quantity = 10        # int
price = 4.99         # float
total = 3.0          # a float, even though it has no fractional part
print(type(quantity))  # <class 'int'>
print(type(price))     # <class 'float'>
code.caption: Writing a decimal point, even .0, is what makes a number a float instead of an int. The built-in type() function reports a value's class so you can check.

blocks.body: The usual arithmetic operators work as expected: + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, and / for division. Mixing an int and a float in the same calculation always produces a float, since Python automatically widens the int so no precision is lost.

code.code:
result = 10 + 3.5
print(result)        # 13.5
print(type(result))  # <class 'float'>
code.caption: Adding an int and a float gives a float result — Python promotes the int automatically.

blocks.robotComment: Three division-flavored operators, three very different results — easy to mix up at first. ➗
blocks.body: There are two special division operators worth knowing: / always produces a float (called true division), even when dividing two ints evenly, while // performs floor division, dropping any remainder to give a whole-number result. The % operator gives you the remainder of a division, which is useful for checking things like whether a number is even.

code.caption: / always gives a float, // rounds down to the nearest whole number, and % gives the remainder.

blocks.statement: Writing total = 3.0 creates a float, even though the value has no fractional part.
blocks.explanation: Whether a number is an int or a float depends on how it's written, not its value — any number with a decimal point is a float.

blocks.robotComment: Strings are probably the building block you'll type most — worth learning their tricks well. 🐍
blocks.body: A string is a piece of text, and Python is flexible about how you write one: you can use single quotes ('hello') or double quotes ("hello") interchangeably — both create the exact same kind of string. It's useful to know both work, especially when your text itself contains a quote character, like 'She said "hi"'. You can join strings together with the + operator, called concatenation — though unlike some languages, Python will not automatically convert a number to text for you with +, so mixing a string and a number this way causes an error.

code.code:
first = "Py"
second = "thon"
print(first + second)  # PyThon

# print("Score: " + 95)  # this would raise a TypeError
code.caption: + joins two strings together, but it cannot mix a string with a number directly.

blocks.body: The much more convenient way to build text with variables inside it is an f-string: put an f right before the opening quote, then write any expression inside curly braces {} and Python inserts its value automatically, converting it to text for you.

code.code:
name = "Ada"
points = 95
print(f"Hello, {name}! Your score is {points}.")
code.caption: f-strings insert variable values directly into the text, with no manual conversion or + needed.

blocks.robotComment: Slicing trips people up at first — that 'up to but not including' part is the whole trick. ✂️
blocks.body: Strings come with useful tools. len(s) returns how many characters are in a string. .upper() and .lower() return a new copy of the string in all uppercase or all lowercase. Slicing, written s[start:end], grabs a piece of the string from index start up to (but not including) index end — and like everything in Python, indexing starts counting at 0.

code.code:
word = "Python"
print(len(word))       # 6
print(word.upper())    # PYTHON
print(word.lower())    # python
print(word[0:3])       # Pyt
code.caption: len(), .upper(), .lower(), and slicing are some of the most frequently used string tools.

blocks.sentence: To insert a variable directly into a string without manually converting it, you can write an ___, such as f"Hello, {name}".
blocks.explanation: An f-string (prefixed with f) lets you embed expressions in {} directly inside the text, converting values automatically.

blocks.question: What does "Python"[0:3] return?
blocks.explanation: Slicing [0:3] takes the characters at indexes 0, 1, and 2 — up to but not including index 3 — which spell "Pyt".

blocks.robotComment: Only two possible values here, but they secretly power every if statement you'll ever write. 🐍
blocks.body: A boolean is a value that can only ever be one of two things: True or False. In Python, these keywords are always capitalized — unlike many other languages where they're written lowercase — and they represent the type bool.

code.code:
is_raining = True
is_sunny = False
print(type(is_raining))  # <class 'bool'>
code.caption: True and False are capitalized keywords in Python, and both are values of type bool.

blocks.body: Booleans usually come from comparisons, like checking whether one number is greater than another. Python's comparison operators — ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= — always produce a bool result.

code.code:
age = 20
print(age >= 18)   # True
print(age == 21)   # False
code.caption: Comparison operators evaluate to True or False, which you can store in a variable or use directly.

blocks.robotComment: Even non-boolean values secretly have an opinion about True or False here. 🔍
blocks.body: Every value in Python has a kind of built-in truthiness, even values that aren't actually booleans. When a value is used somewhere a True/False answer is needed (like an if statement), Python converts it automatically. Values that count as False are called falsy: the number 0, an empty string "", the special value None, and empty collections like an empty list []. Essentially every other value — including any nonzero number and any non-empty string — is truthy.

code.caption: An empty string is falsy, so its if block is skipped; a non-empty string is truthy, so its block runs.

blocks.sentence: In Python, the two boolean values are written ___, always with a capital letter, unlike lowercase true/false in some other languages.
blocks.explanation: Python's boolean keywords are capitalized: True and False. Lowercase true or false would cause a NameError.

blocks.question: Which of these values is considered falsy in Python?
blocks.explanation: The integer 0 is falsy. Interestingly, the string "False" is truthy, since any non-empty string is truthy regardless of its text.

blocks.robotComment: 😄 Compare it to the other empty collections you just read about.
blocks.statement: An empty list, [], is considered falsy in Python.
blocks.explanation: Empty collections — including empty lists, empty strings, and empty dictionaries — are all falsy.

blocks.robotComment: Nothing converts behind your back here — you always have to ask for it explicitly. 🐍
blocks.body: Type conversion means turning a value of one type into another, and in Python you always do it explicitly by calling a function: int(), float(), or str(). Nothing converts automatically behind your back — you have to ask for it.

code.code:
age_text = "25"
age_number = int(age_text)
print(age_number + 1)   # 26
print(type(age_number)) # <class 'int'>
code.caption: int() converts a string of digits into an actual int, which can then be used in arithmetic.

blocks.body: float() works the same way but produces a decimal number, and str() goes the opposite direction, turning any value — a number, a boolean, anything — into its text representation.

code.code:
price_text = "4.99"
price = float(price_text)
print(price * 2)  # 9.98

count = 5
message = "You have " + str(count) + " items"
print(message)
code.caption: float() parses decimal text into a number; str() turns a number into text so it can be concatenated with +.

blocks.robotComment: This is the gotcha that trips up almost everyone the first time. ⚠️
blocks.body: Converting between numeric types has one important trap: int() cannot directly parse a string that contains a decimal point. Calling int("3.5") raises a ValueError, because int() expects a string that looks like a whole number. To handle text like "3.5", you must convert it to a float first, and then, if you really want a whole number, convert that float to an int — which truncates (cuts off) the decimal part rather than rounding.

code.code:
# int("3.5")        # raises ValueError: invalid literal for int()

value = float("3.5")  # 3.5, works fine
whole = int(value)     # 3, truncated — not rounded
print(whole)
code.caption: int() rejects decimal-looking text directly, but converting to float first, then to int, works — and truncates.

blocks.sentence: Calling int("3.5") directly raises a ___, because int() cannot parse a decimal point in text.
blocks.explanation: int() expects text that looks like a whole number; "3.5" must be converted with float() first before becoming an int.

blocks.question: What is the correct way to turn the text "3.5" into the int 3?
blocks.explanation: You must convert to float first, since int() cannot parse a decimal point directly; int(float("3.5")) then truncates to 3.

blocks.statement: str() can convert values of any type, including numbers and booleans, into their text representation.
blocks.explanation: str() works on virtually any value — str(42) gives "42" and str(True) gives "True".
